organism: Poliovirus, an enterovirus in the Picornaviridae family (small, ether-insensitive, RNA genome). There are three serotypes (1, 2, 3), and immunity to one does not meaningfully protect against the others. The virus is rapidly inactivated by heat, formaldehyde, chlorine, and ultraviolet light.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation is 3-6 days for nonparalytic disease, 7-21 days to paralysis onset in paralytic disease. About 70% of infections in children are entirely asymptomatic (though still contagious); about 24% cause abortive poliomyelitis, a mild, nonspecific illness with full recovery in under a week; 1%-5% cause nonparalytic aseptic meningitis; and fewer than 1% progress to flaccid paralysis, typically asymmetric and more severe proximally, with intact sensation and no cognitive change. Paralysis present at 12 months (which occurs in about two-thirds of paralytic patients) is usually permanent. Case-fatality for paralytic polio is 2%-5% in children but 15%-30% in adolescents and adults, rising to 25%-75% with bulbar (brainstem) involvement. Decades later, 25%-40% of people who had paralytic polio as children can develop post-polio syndrome - new muscle pain and weakness that is not infectious and does not involve virus shedding.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only reservoir, with no asymptomatic carrier state except in immunocompromised people; most transmission comes from people with inapparent infection. Spread is via the fecal-oral or oral-oral route, with fecal-oral dominant where sanitation is poor. In temperate climates, infection peaks in summer; there's no seasonal pattern in the tropics. The virus is highly infectious - seroconversion approaches 100% among susceptible household contacts of infected children - and people are most infectious in the days immediately before and after symptom onset, though virus can persist in stool for up to 6 weeks.
secularTrendsSummary: US cases peaked at more than 21,000 paralytic cases in 1952. Inactivated vaccine (IPV, 1955) and oral vaccine (OPV, 1961) drove rapid declines; the last domestically acquired wild poliovirus case was in 1979 (an outbreak in Amish communities seeded by importation from the Netherlands). From 1980-1999, of 162 confirmed US paralytic cases, 95% were vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) from the OPV vaccine strain itself rather than wild virus - which led ACIP to recommend exclusive IPV use starting in 1999-2000, eliminating domestic VAPP (last US case 1999). Globally, the eradication effort has been dramatically successful: an estimated 350,000 paralytic cases per year in 1988 fell to 125 wild-poliovirus cases in 2019 (over 99% reduction), with wild type 2 eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019 - only type 1 remains endemic, in two countries. However, circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV), from OPV strains that have reverted to wild-type-like virulence in under-vaccinated communities, has become a growing concern and has exceeded wild poliovirus case counts globally since 2017.
vaccineDescription: IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine, currently distributed as IPOL) is grown in monkey kidney (Vero) cells and inactivated with formaldehyde; it's the only poliovirus vaccine used in the US today, given subcutaneously or intramuscularly, and contains neomycin, streptomycin, polymyxin B, and the preservative 2-phenoxyethanol, with no adjuvant. Oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV, live attenuated Sabin strains) was used extensively in the US from the 1960s through the 1990s but was phased out entirely because of VAPP risk (see Secular Trends) - it is no longer used in the US, though it remains part of global eradication efforts elsewhere. IPV is also included in five combination products: DTaP-HepB-IPV (Pediarix), DTaP-IPV/Hib (Pentacel), DTaP-IPV (Kinrix), DTaP-IPV (Quadracel), and DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB (Vaxelis).
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine schedule is 4 doses: 2, 4, and 6-18 months, then a final dose at 4-6 years, at least 6 months after the prior dose - a dose given on or after the 4th birthday counts regardless of how many prior doses were given. The recommended interval between the first 3 doses is 2 months; the minimum is 4 weeks, and the minimum age for dose 1 is 6 weeks, but both the minimum age and minimum intervals should only be used if the child faces imminent exposure risk (an outbreak or travel to an endemic region) - shorter intervals or an earlier start can produce lower seroconversion under normal circumstances. Routine polio vaccination of US-resident adults 18+ is not necessary, since most already have childhood immunity and exposure risk is very low; adults at genuinely increased risk (lab workers handling poliovirus specimens, health care personnel with possible-polio patient contact, travelers to endemic/epidemic areas) without a documented history should get a primary series - full 3-dose IPV series if 8+ weeks are available before protection is needed, 2 doses if 4-8 weeks, or a single dose if less than 4 weeks, completing the remaining doses later if they remain at risk.
vaccineEfficacySummary: IPV is highly effective: 90% or more of recipients develop protective antibody to all three serotypes after 2 doses, and at least 99% do after 3. It prevents the virus from reaching the central nervous system and causing paralysis, though IPV recipients can still shed virus in stool after wild or vaccine-virus exposure (unlike in the nasopharynx, where IPV recipients typically don't shed) - it produces less local intestinal immunity than OPV did. Duration of immunity isn't known with certainty but is probably lifelong after a complete series.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication. Because IPV contains trace streptomycin, neomycin, and polymyxin B, there's a possibility of allergic reaction in people sensitive to those antibiotics, though non-anaphylactic sensitivities (like skin contact reactions) are not a reason to withhold vaccination. Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution, as is pregnancy - though no adverse effects have actually been documented in pregnant women or their fetuses, avoidance is recommended on theoretical grounds only; if a pregnant woman is at genuine increased risk and needs immediate protection, IPV can be given on the standard adult schedule. Combination vaccines carry the contraindications of their individual components.
vaccineSafetySummary: IPV reactions are mild and transient: induration (18%), pain (13%), and erythema (3.2%) within 48 hours in prelicensure trials (though these were co-administered with DTP, so attribution to IPV specifically is imperfect). No increased serious-adverse-event rate has been observed in countries using all-IPV schedules, and a 1991-1998 US VAERS review found no increase in reporting after expanded IPV use. Since IPV contains no live virus, it cannot cause vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) - that risk was specific to the now-discontinued OPV, where it occurred very rarely (via reversion of the attenuated strain to a more neurotropic form) but was 7-21 times more likely after the first dose than later doses, more common in adults than children, and nearly 7,000 times more likely in people with certain B-lymphocyte immunodeficiencies.
vaccineStorageSummary: IPV must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance. Poliovirus is best recovered from stool culture (less reliably from the pharynx, and only rarely from CSF or blood); two stool specimens at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days of symptom onset, are recommended given intermittent shedding. RT-PCR and genomic sequencing distinguish wild, vaccine (Sabin), and vaccine-derived strains. Serology is largely unavailable due to poliovirus containment regulations and has practical limitations even where available (paired specimens needed, and immunocompromised patients may show no antibody response despite genuine infection).

supplementalTopics.title: Global Eradication Effort
supplementalTopics.summary: The Western Hemisphere was certified free of indigenous wild poliovirus in 1994 following a Pan American Health Organization elimination campaign; the World Health Assembly adopted a global eradication goal in 1988, led by a coalition including WHO, UNICEF, CDC, Rotary International, the Gates Foundation, and Gavi. Type 2 wild poliovirus was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019, leaving only type 1 endemic, in two countries. In 2016, all OPV-using countries simultaneously switched from trivalent to bivalent OPV (dropping the type 2 component) to reduce circulating type 2 vaccine-derived virus risk - a use of mOPV2 (monovalent type 2) in outbreak response now requires WHO Director-General approval. Despite this progress, circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus caused more than 1,200 paralytic cases from 2000-2019 and has exceeded wild-virus case counts globally since 2017, driven by low routine immunization coverage and gaps in vaccination campaign quality.

keyPoints: First clearly described in England in 1789, but didn't appear in epidemics until the late 19th century
US cases peaked at over 21,000 paralytic cases in 1952, just before vaccine introduction
The US switched to exclusive IPV use in 1999-2000 specifically to eliminate vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP), which had been causing 95% of US paralytic cases by then - not wild virus
IPV cannot cause VAPP since it contains no live virus; that risk was unique to the now-discontinued oral vaccine
Post-polio syndrome, appearing 15-40 years after childhood paralytic infection, is not infectious and does not involve viral shedding
Circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus has exceeded wild poliovirus case counts globally since 2017, complicating the final stage of eradication
Routine adult vaccination is not recommended in the US - only travelers, lab workers, and certain health care personnel at genuine increased risk
